$comment: CodeQL severity policy for agent-cli. Maps each CodeQL rule family to either 'block' (PR fails branch-protection required check on the CodeQL Analyze job) or 'advisory' (SARIF upload keeps showing it on the Security tab but does not block). Updated 2026-08-25 by the CodeQL fix planning team (qa-engineer + devops-engineer + software-architect + external architect peer review).

policy_metadata.rationale: Block rules are real security or correctness bugs (CWE-classified where applicable). Advisory rules are quality/maintainability findings that do not pose an immediate risk; bulk-fix them in the next minor release rather than blocking each PR.
policy_metadata.enforcement_mechanism: CORRECTED 2026-08-27. There are TWO mechanisms and the alert policy is enforced by the second, not the first. (1) Classic branch protection on main requires the `Analyze (javascript-typescript)` context. That context only means the analysis RAN — the codeql.yml workflow deliberately does not fail-on-findings, so SARIF keeps reaching the Security tab, and the job reports success with alerts open. (2) The `main` ruleset carries a separate `code_scanning` rule (tool CodeQL, alerts_threshold errors_and_warnings, security_alerts_threshold medium_or_higher). THAT is what blocks a merge on severity. It is not a status check and appears in no required-contexts list. This entry previously said enforcement was via the branch-protection context, which was wrong: observed on PR #14, where `Analyze (javascript-typescript)` reported SUCCESS with three high alerts open and the ruleset rule held the merge. Reading the required-contexts list alone will tell you the alert gate does not exist. See .github/required-status-checks.json, whose `external` entry for the `CodeQL` check run records the same split.
policy_metadata.review_cadence: On every PR touching src/ or scripts/. Update this file in the same PR that adds a new CodeQL rule family (avoid silent enforcement gaps).
policy_metadata.false_positive_handling: CORRECTED 2026-08-27. This entry used to say "suppress with `// lgtm [rule-id]`", and that DOES NOT WORK. `lgtm[...]` was LGTM.com's syntax; GitHub Code Scanning does not honour it, so every such comment in this repository is documentation and not suppression. Proof: src/mcp/client.js carries `// lgtm[js/file-access-to-http]` at :455 and this file claimed the alert was suppressed, while the alert sat OPEN at :471 the whole time — unnoticed only because that rule is advisory_only and blocked nothing. What this repository has ACTUALLY been doing is dismissing alerts in the Security tab with reason "false positive" (see scripts/add-target.js, test/secrets.test.js, test/inspect.test.js, test/serve.test.js). So the real process is: (1) dismiss the alert in the Security tab with a reason — this needs the UI and repo rights, so it is the maintainer's action, not an agent's; (2) leave an inline `// lgtm[rule-id]` comment at the call site anyway, NOT as a suppression but as the in-code record of why it was dismissed, which is what makes `git grep 'lgtm\['` a meaningful audit; (3) record the rationale here. The rule STAYS in block_on_pr or advisory_only either way — the mapping in this file remains authoritative. A third option exists and was deliberately not taken: a `query-filters` exclude in a `.github/codeql/codeql-config.yml` referenced from codeql.yml. That silences a rule repo-wide rather than at one call site, which is wrong for anything in block_on_pr.
policy_metadata.known_inconsistency_js_file_access_to_ht: As of 2026-08-27 the alert at src/mcp/client.js is OPEN, not suppressed, despite advisory_rationale_js_file_access_to_http below describing it as "suppressed inline ... with a matching lgtm comment". That description was written believing lgtm comments suppress; they do not. The rationale itself still stands on the merits — it is advisory_only, so it blocks nothing — but it should be dismissed in the Security tab if the intent is for it to be suppressed, or the wording here changed to say it is simply accepted. Recorded rather than quietly fixed because the fix is a maintainer UI action.
policy_metadata.suppression_rationale_js_file_system_rac: src/util.js, probeFdIdentity: the lstat-then-open ordering is genuinely racy and the alert is correct about the pattern. It is NOT justified by mkdtemp's 0700 mode — that branch is win32-only (`pre` is null on POSIX, so the probe never runs there), and Windows largely ignores that mode and inherits the parent directory's ACLs, which are private for a per-user %TEMP% and not established as private for a service identity on C:\Windows\Temp. Arguing 0700 would be POSIX reasoning about a code path that never runs on POSIX. What justifies accepting it is a property of the design rather than of the filesystem: only ONE probe verdict helps an attacker — "unreliable", which downgrades readFileNoFollow to the weaker same-family check — and probeFdIdentityCorroborated requires that verdict from PROBE_CORROBORATION (3) separately created, unpredictably named directories before believing it, while "reliable" is fail-closed and taken from the first probe reporting it. Winning one race changes nothing; an attacker must win all three, back to back, at paths they cannot predict. Rule stays in block_on_pr. Re-examine if PROBE_CORROBORATION is ever lowered to 1, or if the short-circuit on "reliable" is removed — either would restore the single-race win.
policy_metadata.new_rule_handling: If CodeQL adds a new rule family not listed here, it defaults to `block` (matches the principle of least surprise — better to surface than silently allow). Add the rule to the appropriate list in the same PR that suppresses its first finding.
policy_metadata.advisory_rationale_js_file_access_to_htt: Inherent to being an MCP client: `agent-cli mcp` reads a server's url and its own Authorization header from a harness config and sends them to that server. The file data reaching the network is the endpoint's own address and its own token, delivered to the party that issued it. The scenario that would make it exfiltration - someone editing ~/.claude.json to repoint a trusted server - is refused by requireTrust(), because fingerprint() hashes url and headers, so an edit revokes the approval rather than redirecting it. Suppressed inline at src/mcp/client.js with a matching lgtm comment. Added 2026-08-27.
